summary.text: 钱 is the standardized simplified form of 錢. The traditional graph combines 金, marking a metal-related category, with 戔, analyzed as a sound component. The sources record both an agricultural-tool use and a money use, but do not establish their historical connection.

formation.text: The traditional graph 錢 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 金 contributes a metal-related category, while 戔 supplies a sound cue. In simplified 钱, these are written with the corresponding forms 钅 and 戋. This is a historical dictionary analysis, not direct proof of the graph’s earliest formation.

components.text: In 錢, 金 is the left-side semantic component, marking a metal-related category. Its corresponding left-side form in 钱 is 钅.
In 錢, 戔 is analyzed as the right-side phonetic component. Simplified 钱 writes this part as 戋; the readings are compatible with a sound role but do not establish its full historical sound relation.

sound_limitation.text: The modern and reconstructed comparisons fit a phonetic role but do not establish a complete regular sound history or independently prove the component’s ancient role.

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 戔 jiān and 錢 qián are similar but not identical; these readings alone do not establish their historical relationship.
In Baxter–Sagart 2014 Middle Chinese, 戔 dzan and 錢 dzjen are similar, a comparison compatible with a phonetic role.
In Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese, 戔 *[dz]ˤa[n] and 錢 *N-ts[a][n] are compatible with a phonetic role; this comparison does not establish a complete regular sound history.

history.text: 钱 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 錢. The traditional graph’s 金 and 戔 correspond to 钅 and 戋 in 钱; this graphic simplification does not itself imply a change in meaning.
Seal-script and manuscript form categories are recorded, but the inspected material does not provide a dated, inspectable sequence explaining how the graph’s shape developed.

uncertainties.text: The earliest secure attestation and a form-by-form graphic history for 錢 remain unresolved.

Modern and reconstructed comparisons fit the analysis of 戔 as a phonetic component, but its full ancient sound history remains unsettled. Baxter–Sagart and Zhengzhang values belong to separate reconstruction systems.

evidence.field: 形義通解; 《說文》; phonetic and semantic components
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 錢 as 金 semantic + 戔 phonetic, with an original agricultural-tool sense likened to a shovel, later commonly used for currency. It quotes the Shuowen definition 銚也。古田器 and the line 庤乃錢鎛. It separately records later currency usage in 《國語·周語下》, fees, coin-shaped objects, and a weight unit. The online entry displays seal-script and bamboo/slip forms, but those image glyphs were not visually inspected here.

evidence.text: Xu Shen's Han-era dictionary defines 錢 as a 銚, an ancient field implement; it analyzes the graph as 从金戔聲 and cites 《詩》庤乃錢鎛. This is an early lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the historical origin or a dated first attestation.
evidence.title: 說文解字/14 - 維基文庫

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the Shuowen account and distinguishes a jiǎn reading for the ancient agricultural implement from qián for currency and related senses. Under the currency sense it cites 《國語·周語下》 景王二十一年，將鑄大錢 and 《史記·平準書》 銅錢識曰半兩, separating those monetary attestations from the earlier tool gloss. It also records the ordinary script component structure 金 + 戔.
evidence.title: [A04311] 錢 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.field: Baxter–Sagart historical phonology; Zhengzhang historical phonology
evidence.text: The page gives Baxter–Sagart 2014 for 錢 as MC dzjen, OC *N-ts[a][n], gloss ‘coin, money’; Zhengzhang 2003 gives 錢 *zlen (with another reading *ʔslenʔ in the entry). Its corresponding 戔 page gives Baxter–Sagart MC dzan, OC *[dz]ˤa[n], and Zhengzhang *zlaːn. These are distinct reconstruction systems and should not be merged. The local Baxter–Sagart TSV supplied for this task independently matches 錢 MC dzjen and OC *N-ts[a][n], and does not supply a 戔 row. The system-level comparison supports a plausible phonetic relationship without establishing a regular sound history exhaustively.

evidence.text: For the proposed phonetic component 戔, the page reports modern Mandarin jiān; Baxter–Sagart 2014 MC dzan and OC *[dz]ˤa[n]; and Zhengzhang 2003 OC *zlaːn. The comparison is evidence consistent with 戔 as a phonetic element, but this secondary source does not establish the ancient referent of the 戔 graph as part of that argument.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No securely dated earliest inscription or earliest use of 錢 was verified. The CUHK entry exposes ancient-script image links, but they were not visually inspected; do not claim a graphic sequence, oracle-bone attestation, or graphic corruption from this research.

The Odes citation supports an early textual agricultural-tool use, but the age of the transmitted text and the exact date of the wording were not established here. A dictionary gloss sequence alone does not establish chronology.

A later monetary sense is documented by the dictionaries with 《國語》 and 《史記》 examples, but the precise semantic bridge from agricultural implement to currency is unsettled. The proposal that spade-shaped money was modeled on a tool is suggestive, not demonstrated for 錢's particular lexical history.

The Shuowen account is an ancient lexicographic analysis, not automatic proof of historical formation. No competing component analysis was found in inspected primary evidence; early graphic variants and possible corruption remain unassessed.
